concepts.def: A large, dark, flat plain on the Moon formed by ancient volcanic lava flows; maria appear darker than the surrounding bright highlands.
A bowl-shaped depression created when a meteoroid or asteroid strikes the surface; the airless Moon preserves craters for billions of years.
The layer of loose, fragmented rock and fine dust covering the Moon's solid surface, produced by countless meteoroid impacts over time.
The Moon rotates once for each orbit of the Earth, so the same near side always faces us and the far side is never seen from Earth.
The lighter, heavily cratered and mountainous older regions of the Moon's surface, standing higher than the darker maria.
The Moon has almost no atmosphere, so it has no weather, no surface liquid water and extreme temperature differences between day and night.

walkthroughs.body_html:
Exploring the Moon — a core area of GCSE Astronomy.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Exploring the Moon brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Exploring the Moon.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: The dark patches on the Moon (maria) were formed by:
options: Oceans of water
Ancient volcanic lava flows
Forests
Ice sheets

mcqs.q: Why does the same side of the Moon always face Earth?
options: It does not rotate at all
It rotates once per orbit (synchronous rotation)
Earth blocks the far side
It spins extremely fast

mcqs.q: The Moon's surface is covered by a layer of loose dust and rock called:
options: Magma
Regolith
Atmosphere
Maria

mcqs.q: Craters survive on the Moon for billions of years because it has:
options: Strong winds
Almost no atmosphere or weathering
Flowing water
Dense forests

mcqs.q: Why do we always see the same side of the Moon?
options: From the Moon shrinking and wrinkling.
Earth's shadow hides the far side.
It rotates once for every orbit of Earth (synchronous rotation).
The Moon does not spin at all.

mcqs.q: Is there a permanently dark side of the Moon?
options: The Moon makes its own light.
The far side is always in darkness.
Earth's shadow hides the far side.
No - the far side receives just as much sunlight; it is only hidden from Earth.

mcqs.q: How did the Moon's craters form?
options: From impacts by meteoroids and asteroids.
The Moon makes its own light.
From volcanoes erupting upward.
From the Moon shrinking and wrinkling.
